21821: If predation is a serious threat to salamanders, and if predation is more likely when salamanders are moving about at night, away from a place of retreat, then it would seem an unnecessary risk for well fed salamanders to move about as much as those which are having difficulty finding food. Juvenile Plethodon glutinosus, measuring 35-50mm svl, of two feeding groups, 6 in each group, were kept in enclosures where nocturnal movements could be detected by infrared beam interruptions. Enclosures measured 35 x 35cm, were 5cm in height, and a single cover object was provided in the center of each. Small crickets, 6-10mm, were given as food every 5th day within the 20 days of recording. Well fed salamanders ate 4-6 crickets at a feeding and gained mass over the test period. The less well fed salamanders were allowed 1-2 crickets at a feeding and either gained or lost mass minimally. The well fed group demonstrated significantly less movement than the group which ate less (t=4.27, p<0.001). These results are consistent with a view that movements outside of a place of retreat pose a risk for juvenile P. glutinosus.

21822: Classic studies of gill vasculature indicate the gross anatomy of elasmobranch gills is similar in most species, and in general, resembles those of teleosts. Studies of fine gill structure of several species of batoid elasmobranchs have, however, reported some structural differences. These differences include the presence, in urolophids (Urolophus jamaicensis, U. mucosus, U. paucimaculatus), of 1) a tip channel, possibly an extension of the afferent filament artery that runs along the top of the filament corpus cavernosum, and 2) a vascular arcade, a vessel which connects the afferent filament arteries of a hemibranch near the tip of each filament. To date, these structures were believed to be unique to the urolophids as they were not found in either rajids (Raja erinacea, R. clavata) or the shark Scyliorhinus canicula. Research with the cownose ray (Rhinoptera bonasus) and other batoid elasmobranchs, however, indicates the tip channel and vascular arcade are not unique to urolophids. Additional research is required to determine the phylogenetic and physiologic significances of these structures.

21823: Hyla chrysoscelis, family Hylidae, ranges from Southern Canada south to Texas and Florida. Internal oral morphology and chondrocranial anatomy for this species have not been described. However, chondrocranial data is available for eight species within the family Hylidae. Herein, we describe the internal oral anatomy using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), chondrocranial anatomy, and ossification sequence for H. chrysoscelis. Specimens were field collected in Beaverdam, Virginia, and preserved in 10% formalin. 21837: Changes in head size and shape during development occur in all vertebrates. 21840: Surface fresh waters represent 0.01% of the planet's water, of which 1% was in rivers, 99% in lakes. Now reservoirs hold five times as much water as river beds and affect flow seasonality. 21841: A distinctive form of longnose sucker, the Salish sucker, occurs in southwestern British Columbia and western Washington. 21843: In his direction to students, Dr. E.J. Crossman emphasizes and encourages a comprehensive approach to questions and problems of fish systematic and taxonomic studies which, at the time I was doing my degree work, were dominated by morphological and osetological approaches. Recently such studies have become dominated by genetic approaches which often rely solely upon tissues provided to laboratories rather than the fish themselves, and focus solely upon variation at the molecular level. Little or no reference is usually made to other character systems such as morphology, osteology, ecology or biology. For well known groups and studies at higher taxonomic levels this bias may not matter, and genetic studies add another dimension to our knowledge. However, for poorly known groups and lower taxonomic levels, working solely with tissues can limit understanding, may bias results, and result in erroneous conclusions. External morphology is often the first clue to undiscovered diversity. Genetic variation may be present but without associated knowledge of morphology may not be interpreted correctly. Thus, quantifying and understanding morphological diversity is important in the development of hypotheses which can then be tested using other approaches such as genetics. Morphological diversity within an esociform (Olympic mudminnow, Novumbra hubbsi) and morphological and genetic diversity within a salmoniform group (Arctic and Dolly Varden chars, Salvelinus spp.) are used to illustrate the need for close association of various approaches to achieve fuller understanding of diversity and relationships of fishes. In keeping with the legacy of Dr. Crossman, I advocate a more comprehensive approach to systematic and taxonomic studies which should include reference to morphological, ecological and biological chararactes as well as genetic characters.

21849: To the degree that a failing memory permits, the presentation will first recount my initial experiences with Dr. Brandon, in Bearcamp Gorge in the summer of 1962, particularly the memorable night of July 4. The presentation will conclude with an examination of the current status of our knowledge of Gyrinophilus porphyriticus in the southern Blue Ridge. Patterns of variation in pigmentation, body size, and life history suggest the presence of three geographic variants. Preliminary research has suggested some level of reproductive isolation among at least two of them. Additional genetic and behavioral studies are needed to resolve questions of diversification and speciation in the southern Blue Ridge complex of Gyrinophilus porphyriticus.

21850: In 1976 James Huheey used a functional feeding model to simulate the effects of adding weaker models to simple Mullerian Mimicry system. Huheey concluded that weaker models decrease the survivorship of the stronger models and have the same impact on the models as would Batesian mimics. This conclusion contradicts a number of earlier theoretical and logical assertions, but has apparently survived the test of time rather well. I used a similar functional model of feeding to ask whether specific changes alter the conclusion that Mullerian Mimicry cannot exist. The newer feeding model included both positive and negative values for noxiousness and a wide range of relative proportions of model species. Individuals of the second mimic species were ADDED to a resident pool of noxious model instead of replacing them. This modification was added because models and mimics only share their appearance not necessarily their ecological space. Success, or lack of success, was measured in terms of mortality rates for both species. Results of the simulations delineate situations with "viable" proportions of "models" and "mimics". In all situations where the second species was at all noxious, overall survivorship for the original species increased. Mullerian co-models have exactly the impact that Fisher suggested in 1930. The model used extended the ranges of possible attractiveness beyond the usual limited range of palatable vs. unpalatable and suggests ways of incorporating these variables into more general systems.

21851: Unmated female smooth newts collected in terrestrial situations were mated in the laboratory, and the ultrastructure of the transferred sperm and the spermathecae was observed at various intervals after mating. Sperm from a spermatophore cap lodged in a female's cloacal orifice can migrate into spermathecae within one hour after mating. Spherical structures on the axial fibers of some sperm in the cap could indicate immaturity. Disorderly clusters of sperm from the cap are still present in the cloacal chamber 12 hours after mating but are absent 24 hours after mating. During storage, sperm often are in tangled masses in the spermathecal tubules. The sperm are coated with spermathecal secretions, and some sperm nuclei were observed embedded in the spermathecal epithelium. Little evidence for spermiophagy early in the breeding season was found. During oviposition, mazes of sperm occur external to the spermathecal orifices, and sperm may be released in this condition onto eggs as they pass through the cloaca. The tangled clusters in which sperm are found from pick-up to oviposition is hypothesized as an adaptation to reduce the effectiveness of sperm competition from the ejaculates of rival males.

21852: Spermatophores of Ambystoma texanum collected in the field from Macoupin and Jackson Counties, Illinois, consist of a sperm filled cap supported by a gelatinous base. This structure is consistent with prior reports for this and other Ambystoma species. Multiple structures consisted of up to 7 spermatophores stacked vertically. Individual spermatophores within multiple structures have a morphology consistent with single spermatophores. Spermatophores within multiple structures adhere to each other. The base of each stacked spermatophore typically covers the subjacent spermatophore cap, leaving only the cap of the top spermatophore exposed. Five spermatophore fields of 21-535 spermatophores were examined. The percent of spermatophores in multiple structures was positively correlated with the number of spermatophores within a spermatophore field (19%, N = 21; 73.8%, N = 112-120; 83.7%, N = 378-535 spermatophores). Further, the number of spermatophores within multiple structures was positively correlated with the number of spermatophores within a spermatophore field (22% of all spermatophores were in structures of 4 or more spermatophores for N = 378-535; 15.7% for N= 112-120; and 0% for N = 21 spermatophores).
21853: Field experiences, from cave bottoms to mountaintops, from the swamps of Southern Illinois to the balds and rain forests of the Blue Ridge and Smoky Mountains, will be discussed. Along the way, previously undescribed forms have been described, studied, and also overlooked. Rare species were sometime plentiful, and "common" species unobtainable. Mimics changed from Batesian to Mullerian. And a good time was had by all.

21854: Although the paedomorphic salamanders Ambystoma mexicanum and Ambystoma dumerilii are not known to metamorphose in nature they often undergo spontaneous metamorphic changes when maintained in the laboratory. In addition, individuals of these species have been induced to transform with treatments of thyroxin. Descriptions of these transformed individuals are based entirely on external features associated with metamorphosis of the gills and tail fin and variation in these external features indicates that many of the transformed individuals are only partially transformed. This study examines the internal changes that occur in the cranium and hyobranchial apparatus in these species in both spontaneous and induced individuals. The degree of metamorphosis in these individuals is evaluated relative the normal transformations known for metamorphosing sister species and spontaneous and induced changes are compared. Interestingly, most of these transformed individuals, whether metamorphosis is spontaneous or induced, die within 5 months of the onset of transformation. Functional interpretations of the internal anatomical patterns are used to examine the possibility that abnormal metamorphosis limits the feeding ability of these individuals, thus, contributing to their short term post "metamorphic" survival.

21855: The Mexican ambystomatid salamanders comprise a group of about 15 species, all of which are part of the tiger salamander (Ambystoma tigrinum) complex. The paedomorphic populations from Puebla and adjacent Veracruz were originally brought to our attention by Ron Brandon, and constitute a system of extraordinary interest for the study of speciation and the evolution of metamorphosis. The region contains at least five lacustrine, paedomorphic populations which demonstrate a wide range of morphological and physiological novelties, while the metamorphosing animals from the same region appear to fall within the limits of normal A. velasci. Based on both allozyme and mitochondrial DNA sequence data, most of these taxa are virtually indistinguishable, suggesting that the ambystomatid radiation from the Puebla lakes region has taken place in the very recent past. As such, it constitutes an example of very rapid physiological and morphological evolution, and possible speciation, as well as severe conservation challenges to preserve these narrowly restricted taxa.

21856: Several important geophysical trends in Mexico and Central America are reflected in the pattern of relationships among lizards of the genus Ctenosaura. The spiny-tailed iguanas are primarily lowland species whose current distributions appear to have been influenced by both fragmentation and dispersal. Identifiable events cluster into one of two general categories which include those which are fairly recent (< 3 mya) or those which are relatively older (> 5 mya). Species or species groups whose divergences reflect relatively older events may have resulted from uplift of interior highlands, isolation of the Baja peninsula and previous isolation of Lower Central America from Nuclear Central America and Mexico. More recently diverged species may be the result of episodes such as the emergence of the isthmus of Tehuantepec, the formation of the Mexican transvolcanics, the fragmentation of Pacific coastal arid habitats and isolation on islands.

21857: Recognizing Desmognathus ocoee as a distinct species is consistent with cladistic and distance analyses of allozyme polymorphisms, but conceals complex patterns of genetic differentiation and significant gaps in our understanding. One difficulty has been our lack of knowledge of the contact zones between D. ocoee and two related taxa; Desmognathus carolinensis in the Blue Ridge and D. ochrophaeus in the Cumberland Plateau. We present data suggesting that the D. ocoee-D. carolinensis "contact zone" is tens of kilometers wide and characterized by discordant variation among several allozyme loci. The Cumberland Plateau populations of D. ocoee are replaced north of the Tennessee River by a form that is strongly differentiated from both D. ocoee and D. ochrophaeus and probably represents yet another distinct species. We are still left with the question of whether subdividing D. ocoee or combining it with other taxa would produce taxonomic entities conforming to any species concept invoking genetic cohesion among local populations.

21858: Rana areolata and the sibling R. capito may be declining in parts of their ranges. Demographic (snout-vent length [SVL] and skeletochronologically estimated age) and reproductive (fecundity and ova size) characteristics were examined in a southern Illinois R. areolata population. Fifty-nine frogs (36M:23F) were sampled in 1996. Hematoxylinophilic lines of arrested growth (LAG) were detected in all cross-sectioned phalanges. Male age averaged 3.53 yr (range = 2-5 yr) while female averaged 3.83 yr (range = 3-5 yr). Male SVL averaged 82.78 mm (range = 71-90 mm). Females averaged 89.61 mm (range = 79-102 mm). Age and SVL were positively related in males (r = 0.81) and females (r = 0.76). Male and female age distributions did not differ significantly, though male SVL distribution was smaller than that of females. Ova from fifteen clutches were counted. Mean clutch size was 4868 (range = 3208-6807). Female SVL and age were both positively related to clutch size (r = 0.87 and 0.64, respectively). Mean ovum/embryo diameter calculated for all yolked ovarian complements, and two oviposited clutches (at the blastula stage or earlier), was 2.05 mm (range = 1.80-2.20 mm). Ovum size and clutch size were negatively related (r = -0.68).

21859: Among tetrapods, scleral ossicles form a ring of small bony plates in the eyes of Sphenodon, lizards, turtles, and birds. The number of ossicles and their pattern of overlap have been used as taxonomic characters for lizards and birds; however, the ossicles of turtles have been considered too variable to be phylogenetically informative. We undertook a more comprehensive survey to assess levels of variability in scleral ossicles and their potential utility as taxonomic characters among chelonians. Ossicles in 432 eyes from 73 species representing nine out of 10 cryptodiran families were cleared and stained. The ossicles were counted and the pattern of ossicle overlap in the ring for each eye recorded. Bilateral symmetry, and extent of intraspecific and interspecific variation were analyzed. Number of ossicles ranged from 7 to 14 per eye. The most common numbers of ossicles were 10 (39%) and 11 (35%). There was a high degree of bilateral symmetry in the number of ossicles present. Within a species, the extent of bilateral symmetry in overlap patterns ranged from 39% to 100%. For the most common numbers of ossicles, overlap patterns were predominated by one or two very common patterns. Although number of ossicles alone may be useful in distinguishing some closely related species, it has limited use at higher taxonomic levels. The overlap patterns are very conservative and therefore of limited phylogenetic utility.

21860: We measured effects of three chemicals and UV radiation on Rana utricularia and Hyla chrysoscelis tadpoles using a center point- and chemical-free control-enhanced 2^4 factorial design. Rana tadpoles were introduced to 72, 500-l mesocosms (90 each) on 25 April 1997. UV radiation was transmitted or blocked using OP-4 or OP-3 filters (installed 16 May). Methyl mercury, chlorpyrifos, and atrazine were applied at 0, 10, 50, and 100 % of 0.4 mg/kg, 30 ppb, and 192 ppb, respectively, on 8 June. Rana tadpoles were sampled 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 days after chemical application. Survivorship of Rana tadpoles decreased with increased mercury concentration (p<0.0001). Size variation (residual of the mass/length ratio) in surviving tadpoles was significantly affected by a UV and chlorpyrifos interaction, possibly antagonistic, on days 1, 8, and 16 (p<0.05) and atrazine (p=0.018, day 1). Fewer Rana metamorphs were obtained under conditions of transmitted UV (p=0.0078) and mercury (p=0.0014). On day 33, we placed 25 Hyla eggs in each mesocosm. Interspecific competition with Rana decreased the number of Hyla metamorphs obtained (p=0.0231). Multiple interacting effects of these anthropogenic and environmental stressors may shape natural anuran populations.

21861: Global trends indicate that amphibian populations may be declining. One of the factors implicated in the declines is ultraviolet radiation (UV). To date, almost all studies conducted on the embryonic life stage of anurans have shown that effects of ambient UV are negligible. Other studies, which focused on the larval life stage, have shown that amounts of UV above current ambient levels may be detrimental to tadpoles. Some anurans have visual pigments sensitive to UV and their ability to sense this radiation may presuppose a mechanism for detecting and avoiding it. A series of indoor and outdoor behavioural tests were conducted in Toronto, Ontario, to determine behavioural responses of anurans to UV. Larval and metamorphosed forms were placed in outdoor enclosures exposed to natural sunlight and sunlight screened with Mylar filters to reduce UV radiation. The results showed that neither tadpoles nor juveniles of Rana pipiens and Rana sylvatica, nor juveniles of Bufo americanus, preferred UV-reduced environments.

21862: The neuropeptide arginine vasotocin (AVT) influences vocalizations in some anuran amphibians but whether this is true across anurans is unknown. We examined the ability of AVT to influence advertisement and aggressive calls in Hyla versicolor. Males were injected with AVT (100 ug;ip) or saline immediately after capture and their calling was recorded. Advertisement and aggressive calls had distinctly different spectral and temporal qualities. AVT-injected males gave significantly more calls of both types at 30, 60, and 90 min after injection, compared to saline-injected males. This difference was due to a disappearance of calling in saline-injected males. In addition, AVT-treatment increased both call duration and intercall intervals for advertisement calls, thereby decreasing overall call rate (compared to pre-injection calls of those same frogs). Aggressive calls were given singly so we could not record call rate or intercall intervals. Aggressive call duration did not change after AVT treatment. Individual animals gave significantly more advertisement calls than aggressive calls. The ratio of advertisement to aggressive calls did not change after AVT injection. AVT thus maintains vocal behavior in Hyla versicolor under stressful conditions. It is likely however that another neural or hormonal factor determines whether an advertisement or aggressive call is given. Supported by NSF #IBN95-14305.

21864: Habituation and its role in the dear enemy effect were investigated in a population of green frogs, Rana clamitans. Green frogs have a prolonged breeding season in which males vocalize from territories to attract mates. We tested the prediction that male green frogs will habituate to broadcast synthetic conspecific stimuli. Our results indicate that male green frogs can discriminate familiar from unfamiliar stimuli. We infer that habituation helps to mediate the territorial interactions between male green frogs. Strangers present a greater threat than familiar neighbors. Males can habituate to the advertisement vocalizations of their near-neighbors, allowing them to focus more attention on the unfamiliar vocalizations of a territorial intruder. This would save energy that could be invested in a male's advertisement calls and in the defense of his territory.

21865: Boid strikes resemble predatory viper strikes. Quantitative analysis of video records (30fps, 1/1000 s exposure) of 160 strikes made by 18 boid snakes representing eight species show that although at least three kinematic patterns may be used, the majority of strikes are made by dropping the mandible and accelerating the braincase over the prey. The snake's teeth slide over the prey surface and do not engage until the prey moves in the direction of the strike. Gape rarely exceeds 60 degrees and jaw closure may begin at or just prior to contact with the prey. The strike terminates with a bite involving ventral flexion of the snake's head during formation of the first constricting coil. The rapidity and variability of strikes suggest that suspensorial design in boid snakes acts in part to absorb shocks. Anatomical and behavioral comparisons to other alethinophidian snakes suggest that the rapid strike may have coevolved with macrostomate gape size because features of skull design that increase gape size also increase shock absorbing potential during strikes.

21866: Pressure/immobilization (P/I) is a first aid method used in Australia for elapid snakebite which consists of elastic bandage wrapping and splinting of the extremity. It has recently been suggested that it be used following venomous snakebite in the United States. However, most physicians do not recommend P/I for pitviper bite because local necrosis may be increased due to venom sequestration, and clinical experience in terms of outcome after pitviper envenomation is lacking. In addition, correct application of P/I requires knowledge of the technique and immediate availability of appropriate materials, its use may increase the incidence of compartment syndrome, and implementation of P/I can delay transport to a medical facility. Advocates say possible increased local necrosis from P/I use is an acceptable trade off if systemic venom effects can be delayed. We recommend the use of P/I in the U.S. be limited to bites by captive Australian elapid snakes and only on a case by case basis. Passive immobilization and immediate travel to a medical facility remain the only first aid measures universally accepted. P/I is not recommended following pitviper envenomation as it has not been shown to improve outcome and may cause additional injury.

21867: We examined the relative stability versus lability of temporal display structure in males of the lizard, Anolis carolinensis. We videotaped headbobbing displays across field and laboratory environments, social contexts, and populations for males from Georgia, Florida, and Hawaii, and subsequently generated display-action-pattern (DAP) graphs of these displays for statistical comparison. Anolis carolinensis is known to be a recent (circa 1950) colonizer of Hawaii, and display from this population could therefore be altered through founder effects, genetic drift, and/or a tropical environment unlike that encountered over the rest of the species' range. Therefore, we expected to find lability in temporal display structure between Hawaiian and mainland populations. In contrast, we found that males from each population used the same three, highly stereotyped temporal display structures (i.e., display types, labeled A, B, and C) in their display repertoires, and that all three of these types were used across all measured recording environments and social contexts. Furthermore, intra-display structure was not affected by recording environment or social context, but within the relatively small total variance, a significant population effect was found for a majority of intra-display units.

21868: We studied perch height and individual movements of the lizard Anolis nebulosus from Chamela, Jalisco, Mexico. Males used higher perches than females. Adults used significantly higher perches than juveniles and hatchlings, and overall, perches were significantly higher during the wet than the dry season. Perch height increased with body, environmental, and microenvironmental temperature, suggesting that perch height plays a role in thermoregulation. Distance moved by each individual was not related to SVL. Females moved longer distances than males, but females remained longer in the study area than males. Significant differences among age classes were found in the time period that lizards lived in the trees. The number of days lizards remained in the area was inversely related with the distance traveled. A larger proportion of lizards that moved longer distances died before the reproductive season, in comparison to those that moved shorter distances or did not move at all from the tree where they were originally caught, suggesting that it is dangerous to move, and lizards should establish soon in a territory to increase their fitness.

21869: Although many studies have ascribed potential benefits of increased water availability during incubation to neonatal survival in turtles, none have directly examined how differential water availability influences the migratory behavior of the hatchlings under field conditions. In this study, we examined terrestrial movements and microhabitat selection of powder-trailed Chelydra serpentina hatchlings from Nebraska and Michigan in an enclosure setting with three different degrees of vegetational cover available. Nebraska hatchlings moved greater distances during the first 4 days posthatching than did Michigan hatchlings, and Nebraska hatchlings from eggs incubated on wet substrates travelled greater distances than did their dry-incubated counterparts. Moreover, Nebraska hatchlings from wet-incubated eggs travelled a greater proportion of their total path distances in areas with low vegetational cover. Though preliminary, these data suggest that the increased water content of hatchlings from wet-incubated eggs may allow them to select pathways conducive to rapid transit, whereas hatchlings with lower water contents may need to restrict activity to areas where local hydric conditions help retard excessive water loss. In addition, differences in movement between the two populations suggest different behavioral responses to water-stressing environmental conditions during overland migrations associated with differences in regional climate.
21870: Parental care is relatively rare in reptiles and cannibalism of offspring even occurs in some taxa. Yet, young often remain near their parents with little, if any dispersal. Using hatchling ground skinks (Scincella lateralis) reared from eggs laid by known mothers, we examined the responses of female ground skinks to each of three conditions; her own offspring, another female's offspring, and a surrogate control. In addition, we observed the responses of individual hatchlings to either their own or a different mother. While the responses of mothers were not significantly different between own versus non-offspring, hatchling ground skinks did associate more closely with their own mother than with a strange mother. Furthermore, females occasionally cannibalized offspring during testing (both their own and another's). These preliminary data suggest that kin recognition of offspring by mothers may not occur in this species, but that hatchlings may exhibit an association preference for their own mothers.

21871: We observed maternal associations between post-parturient pigmy rattlesnakes and their offspring in the field between 1992 and 1997, and in 1997 performed manipulative experiments on 31 mothers and their captive-born litters to determine whether association was passive or active. In 16 litters, females and their litters were housed in divided terraria where females could gain access to their young only by crossing a barrier inaccessible to neonates. In 15 litters, terraria were divided by a barrier passable by neonates but not the mother. Behavior was monitored until offspring had completed their first neonatal shed. Twelve of 16 females crossed the barrier to associate with offspring, 7 within the first hour after separation. This differed significantly from a random distribution of females (binomial test, P=0.038). The proportion of offspring in association with their mother increased steadily with time after separation, and significantly more than 50% (random expectation) of offspring had crossed the barrier to associate with their mother in 8 of the 12 time periods during which observations were made. Association between post-parturient females and their offspring is due to active behaviors by both mothers and their offspring.

21872: To quantify the defensive behavior of venomous snakes, we tested the behavior of 50 free-ranging cottonmouths (Agkistrodon piscivorus) when confronted by a human antagonist. Cottonmouths encountered in the field received one or more of three treatments: 1) one of us stepped beside the snake with our boot touching the snake's body and held that position for 20 sec, 2) one of us stepped directly on one of the coils of the snake for 20 sec with enough force to cause discomfort to the snake, or 3) one of us grabbed the snake at midbody with a set of snake tongs modified to resemble a human arm and hand. The behavior of tested snakes (e.g., tongue flicking, crawling away, gaping, musking, striking, biting) was recorded during each stimulus. Nine snakes escaped upon being encountered and were not tested. When stepped beside, about 50% attempted to escape, about 25% gaped, and none struck. When stepped on, about 50% gaped, and only about 10% bit the boot. When grabbed with the artificial hand, about 35% bit. The unexpectedly low incidence of biting leads to our conclusion that cottonmouths aggressively defend themselves only as a last resort.

21873: Internal transcribed spacers (ITS1 and ITS2) are DNA regions separating the multicopy, nuclear ribosomal RNA genes. We have obtained complete ITS2 sequences from several sharks representing different lineages, and report here on aspects of the comparative structure and evolution of this locus. Shark ITS2 regions are the largest reported for any eukaryote, a size explained in part by the insertion of sequence elements strongly resembling group I introns. These insertion elements appear to be present in all major shark lineages. They are, however, conspicuously absent from hammerhead sharks, arguing for an ancient origin of these elements with subsequent loss in the presumably derived hammerhead lineage. The insertion element is also absent from the ITS2 of the one stingray (Urolophus jamaicensis) we have examined thus far. We have also explored the phylogenetic utility of ITS2 sequences for resolving some relationships within the family Carcharhinidae. The precise affinities of Prionace and Negaprion to Carcharhinus are currently unsettled, with hypotheses proposed about Prionace being either a derived species within or sister taxon to Carcharhinus. Preliminary phylogenetic analysis of ITS2 sequences places Prionace well within the Carcharhinus clade, arguing against the current status of the blue shark as a separate genus.

21874: Most fishes are faced with one of two options for gill ventilation: physically moving their gills through the medium ("ram" ventilation), or actively pumping the medium over their gills via "buccal pumping". The basic pattern of mechanical movements during buccal pumping was studied over 40 years ago. However, unique patterns of water flow through the head of the swellshark during feeding suggested that the generation of respiratory currents might not be as simple as once thought. Using pressure transducers implanted into the buccal and gill cavities of actively respiring swellsharks, it was discovered that pressure traces vary within and among individuals. These data, combined with both video and electrical impedance data for the displacement of the lower jaw and gill septum, suggest that although the classic pattern of pressure generation regularly occurs, at least one novel pattern of pressure generation exists. During this novel pattern, pressure reversals exist over a much longer duration than previously thought possible, and at much larger magnitudes. It is questionable whether the classic alternating "suction" and "pressure" pumps are always used for moving water over the gills unidirectionally, and whether continuous water flow over the gills exists for large intervals of time in this species.

21875: The swell shark, Cephaloscyllium ventriosum, is an oviparous chondrichthyan fish. Each egg capsule contains a single embryo that is incubated on the sea floor for 7.5 to 10 months. The horny capsule material is not sufficiently permeable to oxygen to supply the needs of a late stage embryo, however, after about one third of development four slits open in the sides of the egg case to admit seawater. We investigated ontogenetic changes in metabolic rate and mechanisms of capsule ventilation. Mass specific rate of oxygen consumption decreases as the embryo grows. Early stage embryos have a relatively large tail appendage that is used to generate a water current through the capsule. During development this appendage decreases in relative size and just before hatching the embryo ventilates the capsule by oropharyngeal pumping. In addition to the active pumping, the capsule is ventilated passively. When in a current, pressure differences along the capsule induce flow through the capsule interior. Sufficient water to supply the oxygen needs of a near term embryo will be induced to flow at current speeds of just 0.2 knots. This passive flow comes at no metabolic cost to the embryo.

21877: In the past 15 years there has been an emphasis on validation of age estimates for fish population studies. However, age estimates have been validated for few freshwater stream fish species; with a dearth of published age validation studies for North American darters of the genus Etheostoma. Traditionally darter ages have been obtained from scales or by length-frequency analysis, methods now known to be unreliable for many species. The purpose of this study was to evaluate otolith and scale age estimates for the rainbow darter, Etheostoma caeruleum, from the James River in the southwest Missouri Ozarks. Validity of age estimates was assessed by following the progression of annulus formation at the growing edge of scales and otoliths in fish captured throughout the year (edge analysis). Samples of 10-15 fish were taken by seine in each of 8 months from July 1996 through May 1997. Otoliths were viewed whole and in transverse section, and scales were viewed mounted between glass slides. Edge analysis of whole or sectioned otoliths indicated that one opaque annulus was formed per year in the otoliths, primarily during summer months. High agreement between sectioned and whole otolith ages (75% exact agreement, 99% within one year) indicates that consistent, valid ages can be obtained for Etheostoma caeruleum using either otolith method. Otolith age estimates ranged from 0-4 years. There was no clear pattern discerned in timing of scale annulus formation, and scale age estimates tended to be lower than otolith age estimates. Our results suggest that scale age estimates for darters should be made with caution.

21878: Florida's Fisheries-Independent Monitoring (FIM) program began collecting sheepshead, for life-history analyses, throughout the nearshore waters of Florida in 1993. More than 1,050 sheepshead (653 females, and 430 males), ranging in size from 107-522 mm FL, have been collected in the Tampa Bay estuary. Ages were estimated after the annuli were independently counted six times from thin-sectioned sagittae. 21905: We reported inter-population genetic divergence among landlocked salmon associated with distinct tributaries in Lake St-Jean. The extent of differentiation between one of these populations from the others was more important than that reported among any anadromous populations. Two alternative hypotheses may potentially explain these observations: the lake was postglacially recolonized by a single founding population and subsequent founder events with restricted gene flow, or they may have been recolonized by two ancestral populations that diverged prior to the Wisconsinian glacial events. We tested these hypotheses by comparing the genetic composition with mitochondrial DNA and microsatellites of these landlocked salmon with that of adjacent anadromous populations. We included a landlocked population from Maine as an outgroup. Important differences in allele frequencies, Fst and Rst values were observed among the landlocked populations, as well as between those and the anadromous ones, which contrasted with lower differences observed among the anadromous populations. Population clustering revealed that all populations from Lake St-Jean grouped together and separately from the adjacent anadromous populations. Genetic distance estimates between landlocked and anadromous population from the Saguenay system were as important as those observed between them and the Maine population. These results support the hypothesis of a single origin of landlocked salmon in Lake Saint-Jean. They also indicate that the divergence between anadromous and landlocked populations of the Saguenay R. predates their recent physical isolation.

21906: Phoxinus eos-neogaeus are all-female fish from the northern United States and southern Canada that reproduce by gynogenesis, a form of clonal reproduction. These fish were formed by hybridization between a female of Phoxinus neogaeus and a male of Phoxinus eos; they express one enzyme allele (allozyme) of P. eos and one allozyme of P. neogaeus for each enzyme for which the parental allozymes can be distinguished by cellulose acetate electrophoresis. We have analyzed the expression of phosphoglucomutase (PGM) and glucosephosphate isomerase (GPI) in heart, eye, muscle, and liver of ten or more diploid and triploid individuals (with 5-7 replicates of each individual) of P. eos-neogaeus. Although a one:one ratio of expression is expected in diploid individuals, the expression of the P. eos allele is statistically significantly greater than the P. neogaeus allele in some tissues for PGM, and in other tissues for GPI. In triploid individuals, expression of the P. eos allozyme for GPI is expressed significantly less than expected. These data indicate a difference in the regulation of the parental allozymes by tissue and enzyme that may effect the ecological role of the hybrid species, and may explain how polyploids survive with three sets of chromosomes directing their cellular activities.

21907: Multicolor fluorescence in situ hybridization (M-FISH) is a new technique which allows localization of multiple DNA probes on chromosomes from a single metaphase. We have used this technique to localize different families of repetitive sequences to the chromosomes of zebrafish (Danio rerio) and several species of salmonid fishes including rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) and lake trout (Salvelinus namaycush). Chromosome preparations were obtained from a diploid cell line of zebrafish and from cultured blood of the salmonid species. Cloned probes were labeled with either Spectrum Orange or Spectrum Green using the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and slides were counterstained with DAPI. Images were captured with a CCD camera and analyzed with QUIPS software (Vysis, Inc.). Different families and sub-families of repetitive DNAs were localized at different centromeric, subcentromeric, and subtelomeric locations in each species. These probes will be useful for identification of fish chromosomes in gene localization experiments using M-FISH.

21908: My research concerns the conservation of quantitative trait loci (QTL) coding for the quantitative trait of upper thermal tolerance (UTT) (resistance time in the zone of maximal thermal stress) in commercial rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) populations. Previous research indicates the existence of four major QTL for UTT segregating in inbred lines selected for response to this trait. Individuals used in this study are the result of intra- and interstrain cross progeny of two unselected strains of commercial rainbow trout. Parental fish were derived from the combination of two grandsires and 12 grandams within each strain. Preliminary analysis indicates that major allelic variants are segregating in these hatchery strains for the previously identified UTT QTL. The ongoing survey of this progeny generation may reveal additional QTL allelic variants. Later work will attempt to determine the physiological mechanism by which the marked quantitative trait loci contribute to the total phenotype by assessing linkage between candidate coding loci (e.g. heat-shock proteins [hsps]) and variation in neutral microsatellite markers. The discovery of QTL-associated variance for this trait in strains unselected for UTT suggests that QTL variants for upper temperature tolerance may be fairly widespread in natural populations of rainbow trout.

21909: It has been proposed that population structure of aquatic organisms is determined by the number of environmental settings allowing completion of their life cycles. In this study, we test the hypothesis that this leads to the development of within-river population structuring associated with the existing number of spawning/nursery areas in anadromous Atlantic salmon. A total of 700 alevins sampled shortly after emergence (50 fish x 7 sites x 2 years) were genotyped using five microsatellite loci. Heterogeneity in allele frequency distribution, translating into significant Fst values among all pairwise comparisons of sites were observed for the two consecutive years of sampling. These parameters were lower among inter-annual samples of a same site than among sites. The majority of samples also clustered by sites in a neighbor-joining tree built from chord-distance. These results therefore support the hypothesis that genetic population substructuring in Atlantic salmon may develop at a very small geographic scale, as a consequence of the existing number of grounds favoring survival of young life-history stages. Because salmon associated with such population subunits may develop local adaptations, conservation and management policies should be planned to preserve their genetic integrity.

21910: The red snapper (Lutjanus campechanus) is one of the most economically-important fishes in the Gulf of Mexico (Gulf). Previous analyses of mitochondrial (mt) DNA in the northern Gulf detected no significant differences in haplotype frequency across a geographic gradient and no partitioning of uncommon haplotypes, indicating that red snappers in the northern Gulf comprise a single genetic population. However, differences in mtDNA haplotype diversity among several samples indicated that some level of genetic population structure exists, and that perhaps a more rapidly-evolving genetic character might reveal that structure. We therefore developed a suite of highly polymorphic DNA microsatellite loci to further examine the partitioning of genetic variation in this species. A subgenomic library of restriction fragments was screened with di-, tri-, and tetra-nucleotide repeat and several microsatellite loci were identified and sequenced. Oligonucleotide primers for amplification of loci via polymerase chain reaction were developed. Polymorphism in microsatellite allele size was scored on denaturing polyacrylamide gels. Microsatellite allele frequencies from different year classes and different regions were compared to further test the hypothesis that red snapper from the northern Gulf comprise a single genetic population.

21911: While reduction and loss of external limbs are hallmarks of amphisbaenian evolution, internal girdle and hindlimb remnants in some amphisbaenian taxa have been known for many years. However, less than half of the known genera have been surveyed for internal remnants of the appendicular skeleton and these structures have not been systematically compared. I surveyed the appendicular skeleton in all extant genera of amphisbaenians via the preparation and study of radiographs, dry skeletons, and cleared and stained specimens and compared them to each other as well as to other non- and reduced-limbed squamates. This study revealed that relative reduction of girdle and limb elements is diverse among the group. Variability in bony and cartilagenous components of the girdle and limb remnants appears to contain useful information for ongoing phylogenetic studies of amphisbaenian interrelationships. All amphisbaenians retain at least one bony pelvic element but many amphisbaenians have completely lost the pectoral girdle. Among squamates, regardless of the degree of limb reduction or loss, the pelvic girdle never completely disappears in amphisbaenians or 'lizards' as it does in most snakes, and the pectoral girdle never completely disappears in 'lizards' as it does in many amphisbaenians and all snakes.

21912: The genus Liolaemus (Iguania: Tropiduridae) is the largest genus of lizards in the Southern Hemisphere. Partially as a consequence of this diversity, the intrageneric relationships within Liolaemus are largely enigmatic. Approximately half of the nearly 170 described taxa in the genus belong to the chiliensis group. Within this large clade, several species groups have been informally recognized including the alticolor and the elongatus groups. I undertook an analysis of mitochondrial DNA to ascertain the relationships among members of the alticolor and elongatus species groups to (1) determine if members of each of these species groups formed monophyletic lineages; and (2) address the evolution of viviparity within these groups. I sequenced about 700 bp (167 informative) of the mitochondrial 12S gene for nearly all described and several undescribed species within the two species groups. A maximum parsimony analysis recovered three equally parsimonious trees. A consensus tree of the mtDNA results were then combined with additional evidence derived from morphological and ecological studies. The combined phylogenetic hypothesis suggests that the two groups are indeed monophyletic. Furthermore, viviparity appears to have evolved independently several times within the alticolor group, but only once for the elongatus group, wherein, one species may have reverted to oviparous reproduction.

21913: The amount of genetic variability present may indicate a species' ability to adapt to a stressful environment and can be examined in a quantitative genetic analysis. Currently, numerous conservation efforts are being devoted to determining whether amphibian species are in decline, as many studies would suggest. Therefore, because amphibians are amenable to quantitative genetic analyses and because their numbers may be declining due to changes in their environment, these organisms serve as an excellent model for examining the relationship between the amount of genetic variability present in populations and adaptability in changing environments. Using tadpoles of a single southern leopard frog (Rana sphenocephala) population, I examined the amount of genetic variability among full- and half-sib families with respect to their sensitivity to both lethal (time-to-death) and sublethal (changes in activity) levels of the agricultural chemical, carbaryl. Analyses of both time-to-death and activity data indicate significant differences among full sib families, suggesting a great deal of variability, genetic or environmental, present in the responses to this environmental stressor. There were also significant differences among half sib families in the degree to which activity was reduced by sublethal carbaryl levels, indicating that this variability has a genetic basis.

21914: The Mojave fringe-toed lizard, Uma scoparia, is restricted to sand dunes in the Mojave Desert, existing in 25 known localities. Because of this species' restriction to sand dunes, it has been considered a species of special concern. Many populations are on the decline due to habitat destruction, misuse of off-road vehicles and possibly a significant increase in raven numbers. The determination of the extent and geographic distribution of genetic diversity among the Mojave fringe-toed lizards is imperative for conservation and potential augmentation of endangered populations. Augmentation of the Fort Irwin population is essential due to the rapidly declining population size, which is critical since small populations are highly susceptible to stochastic events. If this population is to remain reproductively viable, then genetic viability and integrity, including local adaptations must be maintained by introducing 'sister' populations; individuals from populations that are most similar genetically. The mitochondrial genes ATPase 6 and cytochrome b were sequenced for 27 U. scoparia from 8 localities, using U. notata as outgroup. In total, 1676 combined base pairs were sequenced, of which 170 were potentially phylogenetically informative. Results of parsimony analysis revealed that the most closely related populations to NTC Fort Irwin are the dunes at Kelso and Pisgah Crater, located southeast of the base.

21915: A phylogeny of the family Lacertidae was derived from mtDNA gene sequence data. Thirty-two species, representing 22 currently recognized genera and subgenera, were included in the analysis. A total of 3,600 base pairs was obtained and aligned from 12S, 16S and COI gene sequences. A preferred tree was selected based on weighted parsimony and functional ingroup and outgroup analyses. Decay analysis, bootstrap and permutation tail probability were used to evaluate support for the recovered nodes. The genus Gallotia was resolved as the basal taxon and the sister group of all remaining lacertids. Takydromus branched off next. All African lacertids grouped together, and formed a monophyletic clade with the Eurasian genera Eremias and Ophisops. The remaining Eurasian lacertids sequentially branched off near the base of the tree in a 'comb-like' fashion. The basal position of Gallotia and the monophyly of African lacertids are consistent with previous hypotheses. The European-origin hypothesis of lacertids is favored, and the distribution of lacertids in Africa is likely a dispersal event.

21916: The zygosphene-zygantrum articulations of snake vertebrae are hypothesized to restrict or eliminate vertebral torsion. This hypothesis is apparently based solely on the inference of function from structure, despite contradictory evidence. Gasc (1974, Mem. Mus. Nat. Hist. Nat., Paris Ser. A Zool. 83:1-182) measured vertebral torsion of 1-2°/joint in dried Python skeletons, but his results are seldom cited. I observed axial torsion during lateral undulation and feeding in Pituophis melanoleucus. To determine whether apparent axial torsion results from differential movement of the left and right body walls, combined lateral and vertical bending, or actual torsion at the vertebral joints, I examined close-up video images of crawling P. melanoleucus and digitized macro video images of torsion in fresh sections of the trunk. To measure vertebral torsion, I clamped sections of 10 vertebrae at one end and twisted the free end by hand; the limits of twisting were clearly detectable and were reached before the movement produced any axial bending. Freely crawling P. melanoleucus exhibited negligible lifting, moderate differential movement of the left and right body walls, and apparent torsion of 0.02-2.4°/vertebra. Fresh trunk sections allowed actual torsion of 0.3-1.1°/vertebra, which produced substantial overall torsion when added over several vertebrae. Therefore, the observed torsion was likely produced by differential movement of the left and right body walls combined with real torsion at the vertebral joints. Despite the mechanical restrictions imposed by the complex articulations, vertebral torsion occurs in snakes and appears to be functionally important in many kinds of snake movements.

21917: Widespread use of agricultural chemicals makes it increasingly likely that non-target wildlife could be exposed to contamination. Many amphibian species utilize breeding habitats nested within or around agricultural areas, therefore population and community dynamics may be influenced or altered by exposure to chemicals. The chemical used in this experiment, carbaryl, is the active ingredient in the insecticide Sevin. This chemical acts through acetylcholinesterase inhibition, and is known to affect amphibian activity and behavior. The objectives of this experiment were to determine differential susceptibility to carbaryl among species, the effect of the chemical under different biotic conditions, and the indirect effects of the chemical. To do this, I used three species of anurans in outdoor cattle tanks: Hyla versicolor (gray treefrog), Bufo woodhousii (toad) and Rana clamitans (green frog). Twelve experimental treatments were manipulated for density (high or low), predator (presence or absence of Notophthalmus viridescens) and chemical level (0, 3.5, or 7.0 mg/l of carbaryl). Results showed that the chemical significantly affected size at metamorphosis in H. versicolor. A predator by chemical effect in H. versicolor was significant; in the presence of the predator, tadpoles at high chemical levels had a larger size at metamorphosis than other classes. Chemical effects on survival at metamorphosis were significant in B. woodhousii and H. versicolor; higher chemical levels significantly reduced survival. The chemical interacts with biotic factors in ways that would not be predictable from two-factor experiments. Chemical by density interactions were significant in B. woodhousii and H. versicolor. This experiment does indicate differential susceptibility among species and noted that differences in biotic conditions affect the potency of the chemical.

21918: In order to determine biogeographic relationships, Parsimony Analysis of Endemicity (PAE) was applied to presence/absence of species of anurans in 14 localities of lowland Neotropical rainforests in the Chocoan Region, Central America, Amazon Basin, and Brazilian Atlantic Forest. Phylogenetic Analysis Using Parsimony (PAUP 3.1) of 340 species led to two most parsimonious area cladograms (TL = 475, CI = 0.705). The strict consensus showed a basal polytomy among three regions: (1) Central America and Choco, (2) Amazon Basin, and (3) Atlantic Forest. Within the Amazon Basin, the localities in the Upper Amazonian in Peru and Ecuador were separated from those in the Lower Amazon Basin (Guianan Region + Belem). A PAE of presence/absence of 108 lizard species in 13 areas in Central America and the Amazon Basin led to a single most parsimonious area cladogram (TL = 156, CI = 0.692). The Central American localities were separated from those of the Amazon Basin. Within the Amazon Basin, a separation between Upper Amazonian in Ecuador and Peru and Lower Amazonian was observed. This pattern is similar to the pattern obtained from the anuran PAE.

21919: A major focus for contemporary studies of natural hybridization is experimental determination of the relative fitness of parental and hybrid genotypes and measurements of the interactions between the genotype and environment. Natural hybridization occurs between two anuran species, Rana blairi and Rana sphenocephala. To determine the relative fitness of parental and hybrid genotypes in sympatric leopard frog populations in Missouri, I examined the performance of parental and hybrid larvae to measure differences in viability. Artificial crosses between R. blairi and R. sphenocephala produced two parental and three hybrid genotypes. Resultant larvae were reared in experimental ponds in single- and mixed-genotype populations. Analyses of variance indicated that R. sphenocephala decreased its larval period length when reared with F1 backcross hybrid larvae relative to when reared alone. F1 backcross hybrid ponds produced more metamorphs when larvae were reared with either parental species relative to when reared alone. When reared together, both R. sphenocephala and F1 hybrids metamorphosed at larger body masses than when reared separately. These results indicate that parental and hybrid genotypes perform at equivalent or higher levels when reared together compared to single-genotype ponds. Such evidence suggests that larval dynamics may play an important role in maintaining the coexistence of genotypes in this hybrid zone.

21920: Remarkable morphological similarity among the cascade (waterfall) ranids of southeast Asia has made them a taxonomic bane for 160 years. Central among this confusion has been the green cascade frog, Rana livida. Inhabiting the fast moving mountain rivers and forests of Indochina, this stink frog has long been suspected of being composed of several species. Recently collected specimens from Vietnam keyed out to R. livida, but exhibited evident morphological differences across populations. A combination of morphology, morphometrics, DNA content analysis, and allozyme electrophoresis was used to investigate whether or not any of these morphotypes were distinct species. The results from this investigation suggested the presence of 5 distinct species. A phylogeny for the group using partial mitochondrial 16S gene sequences was estimated. A 537 base pair region yielded 91 potentially informative characters. Maximum parsimony was used to evaluate the data. Because these species were identified over a very small portion of the geographic range of the Rana livida group, it is expected that this phylogeny will be expanded as more species of this poorly understood complex are discovered.

21921: Deserts are characterized by extreme environmental and resource variation; many desert reptiles have the ability to tolerate these stresses through behavioral and physiological mechanisms. Desert horned lizards, Phrynosoma platyrhinos, are one of the most common lizards in the Mojave desert. Horned lizards are morphologically adapted to exploit ants as their primary food source, and they are characterized by certain aspects of typical sit-and-wait predators. It has been suggested that desert horned lizards should have relatively low energy requirements because of their foraging strategy and because they inhabit an area typified by low resource availability. To address this hypothesis, I used doubly labeled water to measure the energy and water turnover of a population of desert horned lizards over a five year study period. The annual rainfall of the study area varied during the study period such that there were normal, very wet and very dry conditions. This allowed me to examine the physiological plasticity of horned lizards. The results of my research will be presented.

21922: This study contributes to the knowledge of Amazonian herpetology by evaluating the mensurable and meristic characters associated with ontogeny, sexual dimorphism, and geographic variation of the Amazonian tree frog Hyla geographica. The taxonomic significance of the displayed variations was analyzed by evaluating external characters. Four hundred eleven specimens from the following museums were examined: Museum of Comparative Zoology at Harvard, U.S. National Museum of Natural History, and Chicago Museum of Natural History. This analysis included population samples from the following political entities: Trinidad, Colombia, French Guiana, Guyana, Suriname, Ecuador, Bolivia, Peru, and Brazil. Mensurable characters obtained were: head-length (HL), head-width (HW), tympanum-diameter (TD), femur-length (FL), and snout-vent-length (SVL). These measurements were used to calculate morphology ratios for analysis of ontogenetic growth variations. The means, standard deviation, and range of all mensurable characters and growth ratios were determined. Distribution patterns of pigments were coded and recorded for all specimens. The pigment patterns, or absence of pigments were recorded for the snout, venter, dorsum, thigh, flank, upper arm, and dorsal aspect of the head. All specimens were examined for sexual maturity. The variations of the mensurable characters, morphological ratios, and patterns of pigment distribution suggest that the populations of H. geographica do not display significant geoclines and, therefore, are one widely distributed species.

21923: Thamnophis sirtalis is a widely distributed, highly variable, snake which is common throughout much of its North American range. Historically, this species has been subdivided into many subspecies based predominantly on geographical variation in colour pattern, although there is also variation in life history traits and meristic characters. Of the twelve currently recognized subspecies, several meet in broad areas of intergradation which are forms of hybrid zones where there is introgression between distinct gene pools. In order to infer the evolutionary relationship of snakes on either side of these hybrid zones, a mitochondrial DNA gene genealogy was constructed. Cytochrome b was amplified from over 123 snakes representing most of the entire range. A 385 or 780 bp portion was sequenced on a ABI automated sequencer at the GenAlyTic facility at the University of Guelph and yielded 45 distinct haplotypes with 73 phylogenetically informative characters. The heuristic search option of Paup was used to find all equally most parsimonious trees (320 trees, length 126 steps, CI=0.71, RI=0.92, RC=0.65). The resulting strict consensus tree revealed three distinct clades whose geographical distributions are not concordant with those of currently recognized subspecies.

21924: Despite the abundance of studies of genetic diversity in freshwater fishes, few of them specifically addressed the role of habitat structure in partitioning genetic variance within and among populations. Microsatellite loci have recently been developed for Salvelinus fontinalis (Angers et al., 1995) and successfully used to assess population structure within the species. In this study, we analyzed the variability of six microsatellite loci among 25 brook charr populations samples (n=30) in order to correlate hydrographic structure with genetic organization. These populations originate from three Canadian National parks (Kouchibouguac, Fundy and Forillon), showing contrasting hydrographic structure. Considering the general characteristics of these habitats, we formulated the hypothesis that the ratio of interpopulation/intrapopulation genetic diversity will be inversely correlated with the potential for gene flow imposed by those systems. Results obtained supported our working hypotheses. Thus, the hierarchical analysis of molecular variance revealed that the lower ratio of interpopulation/intrapopulation genetic diversity was found in Kouchibouguac (high migration potential) [0.0703, P=0.01210] whereas an intermediate value was observed in Fundy (intermediate migration potential) [0.1771, P=0.00000]. The highest ratio was observed in Forillon (low migration potential) [1.6885, P=0.00000]. We discuss the importance of habitat complexity on genetic structure in the context of management and conservation.

21925: The identification of brook charr conservation units and processes responsible for their evolution are prerequisites to the conservation and management of the species in national parks. In this study we documented genetic diversity among brook charr populations from la Mauricie national park and investigated factors that can account for the variation observed. Thirty-six populations (n=30) from eight different drainages were genetically characterized at five microsatellites and mtDNA. The mtDNA homogeneity indicated a common refugial origin of all populations. In contrast, extensive polymorphism was observed at microsatellites. Eleven evolutionary lineages were identified and their divergence apparently predated the postglacial recolonization of the park, suggesting that the park was recolonized by multiple population waves from a single yet fragmented glacial refuge. Multivariate statistical analysis highlighted the role of hydrographic systems, altitude, and stocking as the main explanatory factors for the observed genetic structure. Altogether, these results suggest that the use of microsatellites may reorient our views about problems of temporal and geographical scales considered in conservation genetics.

21926: We reanalyzed the data of a recently published study of higher-level snake relationships, which was based on a UPGMA analysis of alleles at four "slowly-evolving" protein-coding loci. The distance matrix derived from these data contains a large number of ties, which are not explicitly revealed in many UPGMA programs. Our analyses of these data reveal that the single, well-resolved phenogram presented in the published study is only one among at least 9,999 equivalent UPGMA phenograms supported by the data, the consensus of which is largely unresolved. Additive distance analysis and character-based parsimony analysis of the same data yield even less resolution. Thus, regardless of one's preference regarding analytical approaches, the data in question are highly ambiguous concerning higher-level snake phylogeny. The highly resolved tree presented in the published study is an analytical artifact that was obtained only because the analysis failed to consider equivalent trees resulting from ties in the distance matrix.

21927: Microsatellite variation was surveyed in six populations of lean lake trout and two populations of siscowet lake trout from Lake Superior using heterologous primer pairs developed for brook trout (Salvelinus fontinalis) and Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar). The number of alleles varied from 4 to 21 at different loci. Mendelian inheritance was confirmed for all loci. Significant differences in allele frequencies were found for lean populations from geographically distant regions and for leans and siscowets from the same regions. Genetic differences between southern and northern populations which were found in a previous study using allozyme loci were confirmed with the microsatellite loci. Comparison of our results with previous allozyme surveys and a recent study of microsatellite frequencies in lake trout hatchery stocks and populations from inland Canadian lakes suggests that there is more within lake variation in large lakes compared to small lakes and wild populations compared to hatchery stocks.

21928: The dolphin, Coryphaena hippurus, is a fast swimming, migratory, pelagic fish that supports important commercial and recreational fisheries throughout the tropical and subtropical waters of the world. Oxenford and Hunte (1986) suggested two distinct stocks exist in the western central Atlantic. The southern stock migrates from Grenada northwards to the Virgin Islands and then returns southeastwards in the Atlantic. The northern stock migrates from Puerto Rico northwards to North Carolina and returns via Bermuda. The purpose of my study is to test Oxenford and Hunte's (1986) two stock hypothesis and investigate the possible presence of additional stocks using mitochondrial DNA analysis. Dolphin samples were obtained throughout their range in the western central Atlantic, Gulf of Mexico, and Caribbean by port sampling and attending offshore fishing tournaments. Preliminary results from restriction fragment length polymorphisms of the ND-1 region of the mitochondrial genome will be reviewed. Significant genetic differences between geographic localities provides strong evidence of demographic isolation and indicates the need for independent management of individual stocks (Dixon 1992, Moritz 1994). In August 1997, the South Atlantic Fishery Management Council proposed management options for the highly migratory dolphin fishery. Data provided by this study on the stock identification of the dolphin should be beneficial to the management of this fishery throughout the western Atlantic, Gulf of Mexico, and Caribbean.

21929: Fundulus heteroclitus is an abundant estuarine fish found along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts of the United States. This species has been the subject of numerous investigations of its own biology and has been used as a tool to study xenobiotic metabolism, development, and ecology. Hybrids between Fundulus heteroclitus and F. diaphanus from Nova Scotia reproduce clonally, and thus all individuals are genetically identical. Heterozygosity at codominantly expressed enzyme loci is detectable for all enzymes for which the parental species differ, with the exception of isocitrate dehydrogenase for which the F. diaphanus is not expressed. We have amplified the cytochrome b gene from the mitochondrial genome and cut it with restriction enzymes for which the two parental species have distinct restriction patterns to determine if the lack of expression of the F. diaphanus IDH allele is due to inactivation of a paternal allele, a phenomenon occasionally observed in hybrids. The hybrids share the restriction patterns of F. diaphanus, indicating that F. diaphanus is the maternal parent of the hybrid lineage. Lack of expression of the F. diaphanus allele must therefore be due to a mutation that inactivated this allele or another rare event.

21930: RAPD markers are powerful tools in the analysis of genetic relationships and genetic diversity. Recently, however, questions have risen concerning the inheritance patterns and the reproducibility of the RAPD markers. 21931: Amphibians have been widely used as model systems for studying the early embryonic development of vertebrates. Although much of the early development of all amphibians is very similar, frogs and salamanders differ strikingly in the way they determine the germ cell lineage (the cells that will form eggs and sperm). The pattern observed in frogs is quite different than the one seen in other vertebrates; the salamander mechanism is apparently much more similar to that of birds and mammals. Although the pattern of germ cell formation has been elucidated in a wide variety of species, little is known about the genes governing this process. Because most major embryological events are controlled by genes that have been highly conserved evolutionarily, it is logical to conclude that genes involved in germ cell determination will also be similar in a wide variety of species. Three genes - daz, oct-3/4 and vasa - have been shown to be critical for germ cell determination in mammals. We have used phylogenetic methods to analyze the homologous genes from frogs and salamanders to investigate whether the evolution of germ cell specific genes reflects the mode of germ cell determination (salamanders being more similar to mammals) or the phylogenetic relationships of the organisms (salamanders and frogs being more closely related). Our preliminary results suggest that germ cell determining genes from two different salamanders are more closely related to the mammalian homologues than to anuran ones, supporting the idea that the evolution of the genes tracks the mode of cell determination rather than the animal phylogeny.

21934: Gulf toadfish, Opsanus beta, are poorly represented in ecological studies and their reproductive strategies relatively undefined. Our preliminary investigations into breeding seasons and mating behaviors of a Florida gulf toadfish population have revealed several unique and previously undocumented strategies. Ten replicates, each with 5 nest types, were placed in the field and observed from February until November for toadfish activities. Gulf toadfish appear to participate in a bi-peaked breeding season. Males established nests and females oviposit during the month of May, then all fish disappear until late July and breeding resumed in September. Male and female toadfish apparently discriminate between nest types differently. Females preferred nests with one opening over those that are accessible to the surrounding environment through multiple openings. Males, however, showed distinct preferences between the five different nest types based on characteristics of each nest. Males that occupy nests adjacent to other male-occupied nests appear to have greater reproductive success than lone males, contradicting the traditional view that toadfish are highly aggressive and territorial. Male gulf toadfish do not appear to aggressively defend any territory beyond their immediate nest site, an observation which may explain why males in groups experience greater reproductive success.

21935: Pseudoplatistoma corruscans is a migratory species of economic interest. 21936: A study of bluegill populations from 12 Wisconsin lakes revealed significant differences among lakes in the degree of trophic specialization and sexual dimorphism. 21937: At the close of the last glacial period, only some 15,000 years ago, numerous and varied freshwater aquatic habitats were formed. The threespine stickleback was one of the first fish to colonize these habitats, and these populations have undergone a spectacular adaptive radiation. The threespine stickleback inhabiting nearby coastal marine habitats is the stock from which these freshwater populations were founded. Thus, both the direction and degree of change following freshwater isolation can be inferred by comparing freshwater and marine stickleback. However, the marine form actually may comprise two types: one living and breeding only in marine waters; and a second, anadromous type. At present we know relatively little about whether these types differ in any substantive way. Further, we know little about variation within these types. I present preliminary morphological and life-historical data showing that these types may not be as similar as previously thought, and I compare the level of apparent phenotypic variability with that exhibited by freshwater populations.

21938: The form of the relationship between values for organismal traits (e.g. clutch size) and organism body size has been of interest to biologists for >150 years. This interest has two, somewhat independent foci: to estimate the slope of the relationship itself, and to estimate size-free trait values for comparison across groups. Despite this long interest, there remains considerable controversy over the appropriate statistical model to use in each instance. Most studies use ordinary least squares regression for both, but this is only appropriate when the correlation between the trait of interest and size is quite high (i.e., > 0.9). Such high correlations are infrequent in life-history data sets. Presently, two alternatives for slope estimation appear to be gaining support: major axis regression, and reduced major axis regression. I apply all three methods to a data set for 50 threespine stickleback populations in order to illustrate the considerably different conclusions that can be generated for slopes. Size-adjustment is only appropriately performed using ordinary least squares procedures. Nevertheless, I use a subset of populations to illustrate how faulty conclusions can be generated here, also. No present statistical resolution to this latter problem is apparently in view.

21939: Migrating silver phase American eels were collected from two geographically separated pairs of rivers in Maine. 21940: Gambusia p. puncticulata is a common resident of saline ponds which show high spatio-temporal variability in physico-chemical conditions. 21941: Extreme phenotypic plasticity of the lip was discovered in a population of Gambusia hispaniolae during a survey of fishes to Lake Enriquillo, southwestern Dominican Republic, Hispaniola Island. 21942: Ethnoichthyology is the part of science that studies the relationships between people and fish, including folk knowledge. 21944: Supernumerary, or B, chromosomes are morphologically distinct chromosomal elements that are found in addition to the normal chromosome complement. 21947: The Neotropical genus Hemiphractus comprises 5 species. Frogs in this genus have long been assumed to represent a natural group of species. 21948: In pond-breeding amphibian species, dispersal between demes reduces the chance for local extinction. 21951: The Banggai cardinalfish, Pterapogon kauderni Koumans 1933 has been the focus of the pet trade since its "rediscovery" a few years ago. 21952: Moxostoma spawning acts involve one female and two or more males, and occur by intense quivering into gravel and/or cobble. In trio spawning the female is symmetrically held and pressed laterally to dorsolaterally during oviposition. 21953: Spatial abilities are important in mediating natural behaviors in snakes, such as localization of refuges. 21954: Declines in populations of some formerly common, widespread amphibians and reptiles in Idaho indicate the need for a statewide monitoring program. 21957: Caecilians are circumtropically distributed amphibians exhibiting many adaptations to a fossorial existence including limblessness, reduced eyes and a strongly ossified skull. The pattern of scalation is sufficient to distinguish between genera, and, in some cases species. Data from several smaller individual G. larvata indicate that scalation begins in the posterior annular groves and proceeds anteriorly. 21963: Concerns over population declines and reports of malformations have led many agencies to become interested in inventory and monitoring of amphibians, especially frogs. For two years, my survey teams have conducted surveys of several species in a variety of habitats in western South Dakota. We have found that calling surveys are not necessarily the best census method for all anurans, and they may result in misleading conclusions. For federal lands in western South Dakota, we recommend calling surveys to monitor only one species, the chorus frog (Pseudacris triseriata).
