Species which breed at temporary wetlands are easily overlooked when calling survey routes are designed. Calling behavior also appears to depend on certain climatic factors which have yet to be fully understood. 21964: Home range analyses are commonly used by herpetologists to test aspects of behaviour, demographics, reproductive strategies, and other aspects of ecology. Unfortunately, herpetologists (and other ecologists) often do not use the same rigorous standards when analyzing home ranges that they use for other statistical procedures. Home ranges are frequently estimated using different sample sizes, time intervals among observations, and total sampling periods, either among animals or among treatments. Using simulations and radiotelemetry data from snapping turtles (Chelydra serpentina), I demonstrate that home range estimates are dependent upon these three aspects of the sampling regime. In order to adequately test for treatment effects, home ranges must be analyzed using similar sample sizes and time intervals. Ironically, one aspect of home range analysis which ecologists have attempted to improve is autocorrelation. Traditionally, autocorrelation is believed to violate the assumptions of home range estimates, and so ecologists often subsample observations to reduce autocorrelation. However, I demonstrate that the accuracy and precision of home range estimates may improve with increasing autocorrelation, and reducing autocorrelation may cause more problems than it solves.

21965: We studied a population of common musk turtles (Sternotherus odoratus) in Georgian Bay, Ontario. These turtles occupy the shallow shoreline waters of the many small islands in this region. 21966: Game theory has greatly improved our understanding of animal behaviour, and can be used to predict the outcomes of fights or contests between individuals. 21967: Theory predicts that in polygynous species males should disperse from natal sites more than females because dispersal will promote the ability of males to compete for mates. 21969: Spotted turtles (Clemmys guttata) are listed as "Vulnerable" in Canada, and are similarly listed throughout the eastern U.S. Not much is known about hibernation in this species, therefore information on site fidelity and communal hibernaculum use may be important to the creation of conservation programs. 21975: The relationship between the spatial distribution of turtle nest sites and nest predation was investigated in a landscape encompassing a 12-ha freshwater wetland in west-central South Carolina. 21980: Recent research has suggested that the dynamics of fish populations and assemblages within habitats can be affected by the spatial distribution (i.e., isolation) of these habitats within streams. 21982: The traditional approach in developing recovery plans for endangered species has been to directly sample the imperiled species. 21985: Artificial reefs currently play only a minor role in fisheries or ecosystem management. The most notable example is their use in the spiny lobster fishery. Further examination of the role that artificial reefs can play in fisheries management needs to be explored. An example may be with regard to facilitating recruitment of juvenile and young adult serranid fishes (grouper and seabass) from inshore grassbeds to offshore, natural reefs. Further, artificial reefs can play a significant role in sanctuary and marine reserve programs. Moreover, purposeful and timed exploitation/rehabilitation of fish assemblages through artificial reefs may help sustain both fisheries and fish assemblages. Artificial reefs may not be effective in habitat mitigation where natural habitat has been destroyed. Information on the complete role that reefs play in trophic dynamics therefore needed. Additionally, an understanding of the time and spatial scales necessary to effect management objectives is essential. While, most artificial reef research, to date, has been directed toward fish and fish assemblages, additional insight into ecological processes and large scale ecosystem management may be gleaned through their study. In the future, artificial reefs construction and deployment design should be directed toward adding to our knowledge base to better manage nearshore and coastal ecosystems. Interagency, interstate, and international cooperation are the cornerstones for this endeavor. Both the positive and negative features of artificial reef deployment as a management tool need to be understood before they are generally accepted as a ecosystem management alternative.

21986: A website (http://www.ims.usm.edu/~musweb/endanger.html) has been created that provides information on vertebrate and invertebrate species potentially at risk in the Gulf of Mexico and adjoining coastal habitats. The website was developed as a means to disseminate the results of a workshop on the identification of potentially endangered species in the Gulf and to establish research needs for these species through a cooperative agreement between the US Gulf of Mexico Program and Gulf Coast Research Laboratory Museum. Detailed information is provided for 78 species, including 24 fish, 3 amphibians, and 8 reptiles. Data include synonyms, nomenclatural remarks, distinguishing features, similar species, species photographs, summaries of species biology, distribution, size, scientific basis for assessment of risk, status of gulf populations, and bibliographies. For fishes, online distributional maps and extensive archival records for each species were compiled through the assistance of many collections, most notably those of the five gulf states. These compilations were used to assess historical changes in species distributions. A bibliography of over 8,500 papers dealing with endangered species and related topics is also available, as well as links to other related websites. Extensions are directed toward more structured data collection, standardized online databasing, and inclusion of non-indigenous species so that information can readily accessed for management and educational purposes.

21987: The notochord of the lamprey is a solid cylindrical organ consisting of a cellular medulla surrounded by an extracellular fibrous sheath and an elastic externa. The base of the medulla consists of a layer of columnar cells with an extensive network of rough endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria. The cytoplasm of these cells also contains distinct lipid droplets and a peripheral network of intermediate filaments. The vacuoles in the cells located in the middle of the medulla are reinforced with a peripheral network of intermediate filaments. These cells are interconnected with numerous desmosomes. Lipid droplets and huge deposits of glycogen granules are also observed in the vacuolated cells. The fibrous sheath is made of several layers of collagen fibers. Interspersed between the collagen layers are deposits of extracellular matrix similar to that found in the elastic externa. The elastic externa is an amorphous layer of extracellular matrix that appears to be secreted by the fibroblasts and chondroblasts that surround the periphery of the notochord. There are several differences in the organization of the lamprey notochord when compared to the fine structure of the sturgeon and lungfish notochord (J. Morphol. 1998). These differences may have functional and phylogenetic implications that remain to be determined.

21988: Remoras (Echeneididae: Carangoidei) are medium sized, specialized pelagic fishes, inhabiting the warm water of the world. Remoras are found in close association with certain marine animals and inanimate objects. In all cases remoras use their sucking disc to attach to smooth surfaces. An osteological examination of cleared and stained remoras reveals that the disc is homologous with the dorsal fin of other percoids. The disc is composed of 4 structures: proximal, medial and distal pterygiophores, and the dorsal spines. These 4 structures are serially repeated to form the disc. The dorsal spine is reduced in size and enclosed in the fin membrane. The paired distal pterygiophore forms the denticulated laminae, and also supports the spine. The medial pterygiophore forms the perimeter of the disc, and supports the laminae forming a hinged joint which allows rotation. The proximal pterygiophore supports the entire unit, it connects to both the laminae and the medial pterygiophore. Each of these units is connected to the previous one by the proximal pterygiophore. The remora attaches itself by pressing the disc against a surface and rotating the distal pterygiophore around the hinged joint. This increases the volume of the sealed chamber creating a partial vacuum.

21989: The postembryonic development of the cartilaginous cephalic skeleton in Solea solea (Linne) was observed from hatching to the juvenile stage. Fry were trypsin-cleared and alcian-blue stained. At hatching, S. solea displays no cartilaginous structure. On day 3, the fry exhibit trabecular bars, Meckel's cartilages, palatoquadrates, hyosymplectics, hyoid bars, the first two ceratobranchials and basibranchials 1-3. On day 4, ceratobranchials 3 and 4 form. On day 12, short taeniae marginales are formed on the well-developed otic capsules and the branchial basket is nearly complete. On day 14, cartilage reduction begins as the posterior part of the trabecula communis separates from the otic capsules. On day 18, metamorphosis begins. The tectum posterius completes posteriorly the braincase dome. On day 20, the left eye moves to the median crest of the head and the right eye shifts a bit downwards. Consequently, displacement of the right eye induces a deformation extending to the right pterygoid process. On day 23, both eyes are located on the same side. On day 29, cartilage reduction affects the hyosymplectics; it continues with the first two ceratobranchials on day 32 and with the otic capsules on day 40.

21990: Xenopoecilius oophorus is a member of the basal clade of Adrianichthyidae. In order to determine the size and shape of brain regions in these fishes I used a 3-dimensional computer reconstruction system (TRI 3.10). To preserve the original size of structures specimens were immersion-fixed in 10% formalin and brains sectioned at 30 um on a cryostat. Outlines of 180 serial sections were traced to calculate the volume of one whole brain and six brain regions; olfactory bulbs (BO), telencephala (TE), optic tecta (TO), inferior lobes (IL), cerebellum (CE), and facial lobes (FL). Volumetric estimates from sampling every section were compared with estimates from sampling each 2nd, 4th and 8th section, as well as from ocular micrometry using linear measurements taken under a dissecting microscope. Estimates from section sampling and ocular micrometry did not differ significantly from the complete volumetric values. Estimates from ocular micrometry were derived from the ellipsoid model [V=1/6 pi*lwd] (l=length, w=width, and d=depth), except for the TO, which was estimated from [V=SA*T] (SA=surface area, T=thickness). Estimates of total brain size derived by measuring the linear distance between the anterior margin of the telencephalon and the obex did not differ significantly from estimates derived from weighing brains.

21991: According to Lindsey (1975), pleomerism is a correlation among related animal species between their numbers of meristic parts and their characteristic body sizes. Lindsey found a striking tendency for vertebral number to be positively correlated with maximum length in many families of fish; however, he did not find the same correlation among 36 species of the family Gobiidae in his analysis. Data on the maximum recorded size, numbers of vertebrae, fin-rays (in dorsal, anal, and pectoral fins), and scales in longitudinal row were taken from published reviews of the gobiid species occurring in the Indo-West-Pacific (120 species), South African (107), North East Atlantic (73), Black Sea (26) regions. Not only vertebral numbers, but all other counts appeared to be positively correlated with size of gobiid species in the four regions. Taxonomic applications of this phenomena and possible evolutionary explanations (e.g., life history correlates, structure of heritable morphological variation) are discussed.

21992: Fishes use their pectoral fins for a variety of locomotor functions including providing thrust for rectilinear movement. Most previous analyses of pectoral fin swimming in fishes have focused on the Perciformes, a relatively derived group. In this study we examine pectoral fin swimming in Polypterus palmas, Lepisosteus platostomus, and Amia calva, representing three basal clades of ray-finned fishes. Both forward and reverse swimming are analyzed to reflect the wide range of behaviors during which fishes use their pectoral fins. Anatomical changes which have occurred in the pectoral fin complex include duplication of musculature and the formation of a specialized fin ray to act as the leading edge of the fin. Kinematically, the frequencies of fin beats and three-dimensional excursions of the fin differ greatly between species. Electromyograms reveal differences in the duration, relative timing, and amplitude of activity in the pectoral muscles suggesting that motor patterns during swimming are not highly conserved in these taxa. These data are compared with information from more derived taxa to trace the evolution of pectoral fin swimming in actinopterygians.

21993: Comparative osteology of the nominal species Campostoma anomalum was investigated across most of its geographic range in North America. Considerable variation was found associated with the food cropping and food processing mechanisms (jaws, pharyngeals) and bones associated with the operation of these structures. Transformations in character states (using Campostoma ornatum and Dionda diaboli as outgroups) were found in the jaws, pharyngeals, suspensorium, opercular series, sphenotic, ethmoid, cranial roof and vertebral number. Results from the skeletal analysis were interpreted as follows. Two broadly defined groups were recognized. One, represented by Campostoma anomalum pullum, is widespread across the glaciated mid-section of North America and southward in the plains region. The second is a complex of forms (represented in the upper Ohio Valley by Campostoma a. anomalum) distributed in the Ohio River basin and peripheral areas to the east, south and west. The stonerollers found in the northern portions of the Ohio Valley can be pullum, anomalum or possible intermediates between the two depending on the drainage system. The largescale stoneroller, C. 'oligolepid', distributed in the Ozark uplands is a western component of the anomalum complex that is related to the similar but slightly more derived Tennessee-Cumberland stoneroller. The stoneroller that dominates the Tennessee-Cumberland is the most derived form of the anomalum complex. It has peripheral (extensions?) in the Green River, New River and on the gulf and east slopes. The name C. a. michauxi Fowler might apply to this form. Two of the most recognizable populations within the anomalum complex have smaller distributional ranges. One is found in the Roanoke-James and the other in the Ouachita drainage.

21994: Sperm competition is one vehicle by which males compete with each other for reproductive success. This paper examines sperm competition between the specialized cuckolder and parental male life histories of bluegill sunfish (Lepomis macrochirus). First, we find that the investment in total sperm production is higher in cuckolders than parentals and within cuckolders, males that have higher sperm production obtain higher fertilization success. Second, the longevity of sperm is lower in cuckolders than parentals. The alternative male reproductive life histories of bluegill therefore utilize sperm in different ways to compete for reproductive success. Cuckolders invest in quantity because they always face sperm competition, while parentals invest in quality because they only rarely face sperm competition. We compare these findings to those in other fishes by analyzing differences in sperm competition intensities and sperm quantity-quality tradeoffs.

21995: Sturgeons (Osteichthyes: Acipenseridae) are evolutionary relicts with a wide distribution in the northern hemisphere. The historical biogeography of their association with their diverse assemblage of host specific parasites is explored using phylogenetic systematics and information from geology, paleontology and paleogeography. The patterns indicate historical exchanges with a variety of host taxa and low levels of conspeciation, resulting in small clades of widely distributed parasite species. Sister taxa of parasites generally exhibit allopatric patterns associated with discrete landmasses and basins. A trans-Atlantic track involving Acipenser oxyrhynchus and A. sturio and a trans-Pacific track involving A. medirostris are evident. The parasite relationships also support a historical connection between North America and North Asian freshwater sturgeons (A. fulvescens and A. baeri or their ancestors) and the biogeographical and phylogenetic relationship of A. fulvescens and A. brevirostrum. Based on these parascript studies, it is hypothesized that a former contiguous distribution of Palaeartic and Neartic sturgeons was fragmented by climatic and tectonic events in the Tertiary causing displacement of the lake sturgeon lineage and its association with the Gulf of Mexico drainages.

21996: Surgeonfishes harbor a group of gut symbionts that include the largest known Eubacteria (cell lengths of 30 um to >500 um). Because the bacteria are acquired after larval surgeonfishes settle from the plankton, the fish/symbiont system in the Hawaiian Archipelago and other north Pacific locations provides an opportunity to address questions about evolution of host and symbionts within and among hosts, within and among islands, and among island systems. We have surveyed microbes in host surgeonfishes from Hawaii, Maui, Oahu, Kauai, French Frigate Shoals, Pearl & Hermes, and Midway Islands in the Hawaiian Archipelago, as well as from the Red Sea, Great Barrier Reef, Tuvalu, Moorea (French Polynesia), Ishigaki Island (Japan) and Gulf of California. A variety of structural morphs of the bacteria, differing in maximum size, cell shape, and the number and mode of formation of daughter cells, have been recorded from all sites except the Gulf. There appears to be considerable consistency in morphs occupying particular host species among the Hawaiian islands, but little consistency among island systems in terms of morphs occupying given host species. Preliminary molecular studies suggest local divergence of microbes within a single host, at least for widely separated localities.

21998: Parasites may play an important role in fish life history and mating system evolution. This paper examines parasite loads in a natural colony of bluegill sunfish (Lepomis macrochirus). All 8 parasite-types were quantified in selected tissues of over 200 females, cuckolders and parentals (n=16,438 parasites). Females and cuckolders have fewer parasites than do parental males. Parental males that obtain nest sites within the colony have fewer parasites than unsuccessful parental males. Thus, parasites apparently determine parental male opportunity to breed, and sexual selection for delayed maturation in parental males increases their average parasite loads. The evolution of the mating system and life histories in this fish is therefore subject to forces of selection from parasites.

21999: Lampetra aepyptera is a widespread species of non-parasitic lamprey found throughout the eastern United States. Previous studies have shown that certain populations of this lamprey exhibit heterochrony, by acheiving sexual maturity without completing metamorphosis. A preliminary survey of allozyme variation was performed to evaluate the extent of genetic differentiation among populations exhibiting either normal metamorphosis or truncated head development. The products of 22 loci were surveyed. Highly significant differentiation was observed among populations. A population from western Kentucky (Terrapin Creek) was highly differentiated from eastern Kentucky and Ohio populations, included several fixed allele differences. Because no metamorphosed adults have ever been collected from Terrapin Creek, it appears to be a new paedomorphic species. Furthermore, allele frequencies among the Terrapin Creek size classes were not different, suggesting variable time to reproduction in this population. The eastern Kentucky population (Big Sinking Creek) exhibits some evidence of incomplete metamorphosis. The presently recognized least brook lamprey appears to contain multiple species with a complex pattern of intra- and interspecific heterochrony. Additional allozyme and morphological studies are underway.
